content.text: A terminal is a text interface to your machine.

The terminal you see on screen is an emulator: a window that draws text and forwards your keystrokes. Behind it runs a shell, which is the program that actually reads what you type, interprets it, and starts other programs on your behalf. Distinguishing the two explains why you can keep the same shell inside very different terminal applications, and why changing your shell changes how commands are parsed while the window itself stays the same.

content.prompt: Which command prints the current working directory?

options.feedback: ls lists the contents of a directory, but it never tells you which directory you are in.
Correct — pwd stands for "print working directory" and outputs an absolute path.
cd changes the working directory rather than reporting it, and prints nothing on success.
mkdir creates a new directory; it does not report your location.

content.hint: The name is an abbreviation of three words: print working directory.
content.explanation: pwd resolves and prints the absolute path of the shell's working directory. It is the safest command to run before anything that modifies files.

feedback.correct: That is the one to run before any destructive command.
feedback.incorrect: Re-read what each command changes versus what it reports.

content.prompt: Which commands report information without modifying the filesystem?
content.explanation: pwd, ls and whoami are read-only: they inspect and print. rm deletes and mkdir creates, so both change the filesystem.

feedback.correct: Exactly — all three only read state.
feedback.incorrect: Separate the commands that report from the commands that change something.

content.prompt: Which command lists the files in a directory?
content.explanation: ls lists directory entries. The default comparison is case-insensitive and trims surrounding whitespace, so "LS" and "  ls  " are both accepted here.

feedback.correct: Accepted — the default comparison ignores case and surrounding spaces.
feedback.incorrect: The answer is a single two-letter command.

content.prompt: Type the long-listing form of the list command, with its flag.
content.hint: The flag is a single lowercase letter after a hyphen.
content.explanation: Comparison is exact, so case matters: "LS -L" is rejected. Normalisation still runs first, so "  ls   -l  " is accepted — extra spacing is collapsed before the comparison.

feedback.correct: Correct, and note that the extra spacing form is accepted too.
feedback.incorrect: Check the case: exact comparison is case-sensitive.

content.prompt: A directory contains exactly three entries. How many does ls print?
content.explanation: Numeric comparison parses both sides as numbers, so "3" and "3.0" are equivalent. Text that is not a number is simply incorrect.

feedback.incorrect: Enter the number of entries as a digit.

content.prompt: A timing script reports 3.05 seconds. Enter the measured duration in seconds.
content.hint: Anything within a tenth of a second of 3 is accepted.
content.explanation: With tolerance 0.1, any value from 2.9 to 3.1 is accepted. 3.5 is outside the tolerance and is rejected.

content.prompt: In one sentence, describe how you would see what a directory holds. Your answer must mention the command name.
content.hint: Name the two-letter listing command somewhere in your sentence.
content.explanation: Substring comparison checks that your answer mentions the key idea. It is always case-insensitive, so "Run LS in the folder" also matches.

feedback.correct: Good — the key command was mentioned.
feedback.incorrect: Mention the listing command by name in your sentence.
